It is built for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Board and batten calculator work?
sections.html:
The Board and batten calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports wall height in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the board spacing, number of doors, the door width and number of windows.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Board and batten calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Wall height=2 × rows of furring strip − 2
Furring strip=wall width × rounded up, (rows of furring strip)
Board width=(-board spacing × number of boards + board spacing + 12 × wall width) ÷ number of boards
Number of battens=rounded up, (number of boards) − 1
Window height=(-board material − door height × number of doors × door width + wall height × rounded up, (number of boards)) ÷ (number of windows × window width)
Window height=(-batten material − door height × number of doors × door width + wall height × rounded up, (rounded up, (number of boards) − 1)) ÷ (number of windows × window width)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Number of doors = 0, Door height = 213 m, Door width = 152 m and Number of windows = 0. The calculator returns Wall height = 1800 m.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Wall height = 1800 m should be roughly the size you expected from Number of doors = 0 and Door height = 213 m.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Area, opening in square meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Board and batten calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the board spacing, number of doors and the door width — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Board and batten calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns wall height, derived from the board spacing, number of doors and the door width. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Board and batten calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the board spacing, number of doors, the door width and number of windows, which is 11 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter wall width in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Wall width opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Wall height = 1800 m. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Board and batten calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
